lines.text: Fabrics and textiles are the raw materials of fashion — their properties determine how garments look, feel, move, and last. Natural fibres come from plants or animals: cotton (soft, breathable, absorbent), linen (cool, textured, prone to creasing), silk (luxurious, lustrous, delicate), and wool (warm, resilient, naturally moisture-wicking). Synthetic fibres are manufactured chemically: polyester (durable, wrinkle-resistant, quick-drying), nylon (strong, elastic, lightweight), and acrylic (soft, warm, affordable — often used as a wool alternative). Semi-synthetic fibres like viscose (rayon) and lyocell (Tencel) are derived from natural cellulose but processed chemically — combining some benefits of both categories. The weave — how threads interlace — determines a fabric's texture and behaviour. Plain weave (simple over-under) creates crisp fabrics like poplin and muslin. Twill weave (diagonal pattern) produces durable fabrics like denim and gabardine. Satin weave (long floating threads) creates smooth, glossy surfaces. Knitted fabrics (jersey, ribbing, interlock) stretch and recover — essential for comfortable, body-hugging garments. The weight of a fabric — measured in grams per square metre (GSM) — determines its suitability: lightweight voile for summer blouses, medium-weight cotton for everyday shirts, and heavyweight tweed for winter coats. Understanding fabric is fundamental to making informed choices about clothing quality, care, and sustainability.
